CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay inside the G20 90-day window and keep talking. Offer a large, verifiable purchase package on agriculture, energy, and manufactured goods to buy time and test U.S. willingness to keep List 3 at 10%, but do not lock in structural concessions on industrial policy, SOEs, or tech transfer at this mid-level round. Do not add new tariffs or further hostage-style moves while talks are live; treat Meng as a separate legal/sovereignty track and avoid letting it collapse the trade channel.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. The United States already covers ~$250B of Chinese goods (Lists 1–3), and the suspended Jan 1 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is still queued for ~2 March if no deal is reached. That sits on top of firm-level tech pressure: the April 2018 ZTE denial order and the 1 Dec 2018 arrest of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou the same day as the G20 truce, plus widening allied skepticism of Huawei 5G. China’s factory sector is already weakening into that cliff: official manufacturing PMI fell to 49.4 in December (first contraction in ~2.5 years; new export orders 46.6, seventh month of contraction), export growth slowed from 14–16% in Sep/Oct to 5.4% in November, Q3 GDP was 6.5%, and car sales are falling. Front-loading has delayed, not removed, the tariff hit. This matches the CHN +0.5 anchor (major export sectors, Huawei targeting, export-hub risk) rather than +1.0: talks are open, the hike is paused, and there is no evidence yet of a reserves/FX or legitimacy crisis. Action should therefore be mild and commercial, not escalatory. The 7–9 Jan Beijing round already showed the only tractable gap is purchases (soy, energy, GM-crop approvals) while the two sides remain far apart on IP, forced tech transfer, and enforcement. Escalating now would likely hand Washington a pretext to implement the 25% hike against a contracting PMI; full rollback or a locked purchase/structural package is premature because the U.S. has offered no matching tariff relief and China Daily has already drawn a public line against “unreasonable concessions.” Negotiate, signal purchases, hold the industrial-policy core.
key_factors: US Section 301 coverage already ~$250B; List 3 10%→25% hike still scheduled ~2 March if talks fail
Huawei/Meng arrest plus earlier ZTE denial order = firm-level tech containment, not just tariffs
China manufacturing PMI 49.4 in Dec 2018; export orders contracting; Nov export growth slowed to 5.4%
G20 90-day truce is live; 7–9 Jan Beijing talks made progress on purchases, not on structural/IP/enforcement
Further Chinese escalation would risk collapsing the window; locked structural concessions or full rollback are premature without U.S. matching relief

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
G20: 90-day negotiation window; planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou on a US extradition request.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). Major non-tariff escalation.
Trade talks resume in Beijing (working / mid-level). China discusses increased purchases of US goods; structural issues remain open.
Official manufacturing PMI 49.4 in December, weakest since Feb 2016; new export orders 46.6, seventh straight month of contraction.
China export growth dropped from 14.4% in September and 15.6% in October to 5.4% in November; analysts expect the tariff hit to intensify in 2019 as front-loading fades.
Jan 2019 talks extended; progress on farm/energy purchases and market access; still divided on structural reforms and how to hold Beijing to promises. If no deal by 2 March, List 3 rises to 25%.
China Daily: Beijing will not make 'unreasonable concessions'; goodwill gestures include GM-crop approvals and another large U.S. soybean purchase.
U.S. imports from China fell from $47.8B in Aug 2018 to $41.3B in Jan 2019 (−13.6%), consistent with fading front-loading into the tariff regime.
